questions.question: What prompted changes in the State Co-operative Societies Acts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Poor quality of functioning**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The changes in the State Co-operative Societies Acts were prompted by the **poor quality of functioning** of several co-operative societies.
 
• Many co-operative societies faced issues like **inefficiency, mismanagement, and lack of accountability**, which necessitated reforms in their governance structures.
 
• The poor performance of co-operative societies led to **inadequate service delivery** to their members and stakeholders.
 
• To address these challenges, the State Co-operative Societies Acts were modified to introduce measures such as **better financial monitoring, improved governance, and stricter audit processes**.
 
• These reforms aimed to **restore trust and improve the operational efficiency** of co-operative societies across the states.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Co-operative Societies:**

 
 
• Co-operative societies are organizations formed by individuals with a common interest, primarily to meet their economic, social, and cultural needs.
 
• They are governed by the **Co-operative Societies Act, 1912**, and respective State Acts.
 
• Their core principles include **voluntary membership, democratic decision-making, and equitable distribution of benefits**.
 
 
 
• **Common Issues in Co-operative Societies:**
 
 
• Lack of professionalism and skilled management often results in **inefficient operations**.
 
• Instances of corruption and political interference have led to **misuse of resources**.
 
• Inadequate financial oversight and poor audit mechanisms result in **fraudulent practices**.
 
 
 
• **Reforms in Co-operative Sector:**
 
 
• Efforts like the **97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011**, sought to improve transparency and democratic governance in co-operatives.
 
• Provisions were added to ensure **regular elections, proper audits, and member empowerment**.
 
• State-level reforms often focus on **reducing political interference** and improving operational efficiency.
 
 
 
• **Role of NABARD:**
 
 
• The **National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)** provides financial and technical support to co-operative institutions.
 
• It also works on **capacity building and institutional strengthening** of co-operatives.

questions.question: Which languages were added to the Eighth Schedule by the 71st Amendment Act, 1992?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **71st Amendment Act of 1992** added three languages—**Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali**—to the** Eighth Schedule** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Eighth Schedule initially included 14 languages, but subsequent amendments increased the number to the current total of 22.
 
• These three languages were added to recognize and promote linguistic diversity and cultural heritage in India.
 
• The amendment reflects the government's commitment to safeguarding minority languages and ensuring their representation in governance and education.
 
• With the inclusion of these languages, the Eighth Schedule serves as a framework for developing official language policies at both the state and national levels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Eighth Schedule of the Constitution:**

 
 
• The Eighth Schedule lists the languages recognized by the Constitution of India for official purposes.
 
• It originally included 14 languages, but subsequent amendments have expanded the list to 22 languages.
 
• Languages included in the Eighth Schedule are eligible for development under the aegis of the government.
 
 
 
• **71st Amendment Act, 1992:**
 
 
• It was enacted by the Parliament of India to amend the Constitution.
 
• The primary purpose was to include Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali in the Eighth Schedule.
 
• This amendment underscores the importance of linguistic diversity in India's multicultural society.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Scheduled Languages:**
 
 
• Scheduled languages receive recognition and support for their preservation and development.
 
• They play a vital role in governance, education, and cultural identity.
 
• Languages in the Eighth Schedule can be used for official communication at the state and central levels.
 
 
 
• **Linguistic Amendments in India:**
 
 
• India has witnessed multiple constitutional amendments to recognize and support regional languages.
 
• For example, Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment Act in 1967, and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santali were added by the 92nd Amendment Act in 2003.
 
• These amendments reflect the dynamic and evolving nature of India's linguistic landscape.

questions.question: Which Indian Constitutional Amendment Act has NOT amended anything in the Directive Principles of the State Policy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**48th Amendment Act**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **48th Amendment Act** of 1984 did not amend any provisions related to the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• This amendment was enacted to extend the President's Rule in the state of Punjab beyond the one-year limit prescribed under Article 356(5) of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It dealt specifically with the political situation in Punjab and had no relevance to the Directive Principles of State Policy.
 
• In contrast, amendments like the **42nd Amendment Act** and **86th Amendment Act** directly addressed and modified provisions of the DPSP.
 
• The **42nd Amendment Act**, for instance, added new principles, while the **86th Amendment Act** integrated the right to education for children under Article 21A, influencing related DPSPs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• Enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution, DPSPs aim to establish a welfare state by guiding the government in policy-making.
 
• They are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced in a court of law, but they are fundamental in governance.
 
• Examples include provisions for social welfare, equitable distribution of resources, and environmental conservation.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act (1976):**
 
 
• Known as the "Mini-Constitution," it made significant changes to the DPSP.
 
• Added Articles 39A (Equal justice and free legal aid), 43A (Workers' participation in management), and 48A (Protection of the environment).
 
• Shifted the focus towards socialism and environmental sustainability.
 
 
 
• **86th Amendment Act (2002):**
 
 
• Introduced Article 21A, making the right to education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14 years.
 
• Modified Article 45 under DPSP to focus on early childhood care for children below six years.
 
 
 
• **97th Amendment Act (2011):**
 
 
• Added a new DPSP under Article 43B, emphasizing the promotion of cooperative societies.
 
• Aimed to strengthen cooperative movements in India by ensuring their democratic functioning.

questions.question: Which organisation does the Ministry of Rural Development cooperate with for rural development in Asia and the Pacific?

options.text: Centre on Integrated Rural Development for Asia and Pacific (CIRDAP)

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Centre on Integrated Rural Development for Asia and Pacific (CIRDAP)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Ministry of Rural Development in India collaborates with the **Centre on Integrated Rural Development for Asia and the Pacific (CIRDAP)** to advance rural development initiatives in the Asia-Pacific region.
 
• CIRDAP was established in **1979** at the initiative of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations to promote integrated rural development.
 
• The organization has its headquarters in **Dhaka, Bangladesh**, and works with member countries to strengthen rural development policies and practices.
 
• India is a founding member of CIRDAP and actively contributes to its programs focusing on poverty alleviation, sustainable agriculture, and rural infrastructure development.
 
• CIRDAP functions as a platform for knowledge-sharing, capacity-building, and technical cooperation among its **15 member countries**, including India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and others.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **CIRDAP Member Countries**

 
 
• CIRDAP has **15 member countries**, which include Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Indonesia, Iran, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Thailand, and Vietnam.
 
• These countries collaborate on rural development strategies and share best practices to improve living conditions in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Integrated Rural Development**
 
 
• Integrated rural development involves a holistic approach to improving economic, social, and environmental conditions in rural areas.
 
• It focuses on sectors such as agriculture, education, health, infrastructure, and community participation to ensure sustainable development.
 
 
 
• **Role of FAO**
 
 
• The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations was instrumental in the establishment of CIRDAP, emphasizing its commitment to eradicating hunger and promoting rural development globally.
 
• FAO continues to provide technical support and guidance to CIRDAP and its member countries.
 
 
 
• **India and CIRDAP**
 
 
• India’s Ministry of Rural Development plays a pivotal role in supporting CIRDAP by offering expertise, resources, and research inputs.
 
• India often hosts training programs, workshops, and conferences under the aegis of CIRDAP to foster regional cooperation in rural development.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the Gram Panchayat in the Panchayati Raj System in India?

options.text: To conduct provincial elections, helping the Election Commission
To act as the judicial forum for local disputes
To serve as the executive body of village self-government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To serve as the executive body of village self-government**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gram Panchayat is the **basic unit of local self-governance** in rural India under the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• It acts as the **executive body** responsible for implementing development programs and schemes for the welfare of the village.
 
• Key responsibilities include **maintaining village infrastructure, sanitation, water supply, and public health**.
 
• Gram Panchayats are headed by the elected representative known as the **Sarpanch**, assisted by other members.
 
• It also plays a role in ensuring **community participation and governance** at the grassroots level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panchayati Raj System:**

 
 
• It is a three-tier system of governance comprising **Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (block level), and Zila Parishad (district level)**.
 
• It was institutionalized through the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992**.
 
• This system aims to **decentralize governance** and enhance democratic participation at the grassroots level.
 
 
 
• **Funding of Gram Panchayats:**
 
 
• Gram Panchayats receive funds through **taxes, government grants, and contributions from villagers**.
 
• Central and state governments provide financial assistance under schemes like **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)**.
 
 
 
• **Sarpanch:**
 
 
• The Sarpanch is the elected head of the Gram Panchayat and acts as the **primary decision-maker and representative**.
 
• They are responsible for presiding over meetings and ensuring the execution of resolutions passed by the Panchayat.
 
 
 
• **Gram Sabha:**
 
 
• The Gram Sabha consists of all registered voters in the village and serves as the **general assembly of the village**.
 
• It plays a crucial role in **decision-making and oversight** of the Gram Panchayat's activities.

questions.question: Which agreement is linked to the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Assam Accord**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Assam Accord** was signed on **15 August 1985** between the Government of India and leaders of the Assam Movement.
 
• The accord aimed to address the issue of **illegal immigration** into Assam, particularly from neighboring countries like Bangladesh.
 
• The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985 was introduced as a result of the Assam Accord, amending the Citizenship Act, 1955.
 
• The Assam Accord defined specific cut-off dates for identifying and deporting **illegal immigrants**. People who entered Assam after **March 24, 1971** were to be identified and deported.
 
• The accord also provided for the protection of **Assamese cultural identity**, language, and heritage while addressing the concerns of indigenous communities.
 
• It led to the establishment of mechanisms to detect and deport foreigners, including the formation of **Foreigners' Tribunals**.
 
• The Assam Accord continues to be a cornerstone in debates surrounding **citizenship and immigration policies** in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• ** Shimla Agreement**__

 __
 
• The **Shimla Agreement** was signed on **2 July 1972** between **India and Pakistan** following the Indo-Pak war of 1971.
 
• It aimed at restoring peace and normalizing relations between the two nations.
 
• The agreement established the **Line of Control (LoC)** in Jammu and Kashmir.
 
• It holds significance in the context of India's foreign policy and relations with Pakistan but is unrelated to the issue of citizenship or immigration.
 
 
 
• **Indo-Sri Lanka Pact**__
 __
 
• The **Indo-Sri Lanka Pact**, also known as the **Rajiv Gandhi-Jayewardene Accord**, was signed in **1987**.
 
• It aimed at resolving the **Sri Lankan Civil War** and ensuring the rights of Tamil minorities in Sri Lanka.
 
• The pact led to the deployment of the **Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF)** in Sri Lanka.
 
• While significant in the context of international relations, it is not connected to the citizenship issues addressed by the Assam Accord.
 
 
 
• **Kashmir Agreement**__
 
 
• The term **Kashmir Agreement** often refers to attempts or discussions to resolve the issue of **Jammu and Kashmir** between India and Pakistan.
 
• It pertains to territorial disputes and regional autonomy rather than citizenship or immigration-related concerns.
 
• It holds importance in the geopolitical context but is unrelated to the Assam Accord or the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements correctly describe(s) the 'Gorakhnath Sharma vs. State of Chhattisgarh' case, as ruled by the Chhattisgarh High Court in February 2025?

1. The case involved allegations of brutal non-consensual sexual assault by a husband on his wife, leading to her death.

2. The Chhattisgarh High Court convicted the husband and awarded maximum punishment in the case of rape.
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Only 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **'Gorakhnath Sharma vs. State of Chhattisgarh' **case involved allegations of** brutal non-consensual sexual** assault by a husband on his wife, leading to her death. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

 
 
• The case did involve **allegations of brutal non-consensual sexual assault** by the husband on his wife.
 
• The** wife died** in this case, and her death was linked to the **sexual assault.**
 
• However, the focus of the ruling was primarily on the application of **marital rape** laws and whether the actions of the husband constituted rape, which leads us to the second statement.
 
 
 
• Contrary to the statement, the **Chhattisgarh High Court acquitted the husband**. The court **did not convict him** for rape, as it applied **Exception 2 to Section 375** of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
 
• This exception exempts a husband from being charged with rape for sexual intercourse with his wife, provided the wife is not under 15 years of age.
 
• In this case, the court ruled that **the husband could not be convicted of rape** or other charges like **unnatural sexual offenses** because of the exception in the law.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__**Gorakhnath Sharma vs. State of Chhattisgarh:**__

__
 
• Case Summary:

 
 
• The case involved allegations of brutal non-consensual sexual assault by the husband on his wife, which ultimately led to her death.
 
• Chhattisgarh High Court acquitted the husband, citing Exception 2 to Section 375 of the IPC, which exempts husbands from being convicted of rape if the wife is above 15 years of age.
 
 
 
• Implications:
 
 
• The ruling has sparked debate on marital rape laws in India.
 
• It highlights the legal gap in addressing non-consensual sex in marriage, where the law still treats marital rape as legal in certain circumstances.
 
• The case points to the need for legal reforms regarding the criminalization of marital rape.
 
 

Status of Marital Rape in India:__

__
 
• Legal Position:

 
 
• Marital rape is not criminalized in India, except for cases where the wife is under the age of 15.
 
• The Indian Penal Code (IPC), under Section 375, considers marital rape legal when the wife is above 15 years of age.
 
 
 
• Debate:
 
 
• There is strong public debate and activism pushing for changes to recognize marital rape as a criminal offense.
 
• Legal experts, women’s rights groups, and the UN have called for a reform in Indian law to criminalize marital rape, but no changes have been made in the law so far.
 
 

Recent Changes:__

 
• 2015: Supreme Court ruled that sexual intercourse with a wife below 15 years is rape.
 
• 2017: Law Commission of India recommended criminalizing marital rape, but the recommendation was not implemented.
 
• 2021: Delhi High Court raised concerns over marital rape but did not rule on the issue.
 
• Current Status:
 
 
• Despite growing calls for reform, marital rape remains not criminalized in India.

questions.question: In the ministerial hierarchy in India, Ministers of State generally have:

options.text: . no executive responsibility in any of the portfolios
secondary rank within the portfolios assigned to Cabinet Ministers
equal standing with Cabinet Ministers in their assigned portfolios

questions.solution:

• In the **ministerial hierarchy** of India, the **Ministers of State** are junior ministers who work under the supervision of **Cabinet Ministers**.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India deals with the application of the Directive Principles of the State Policy?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 37**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 37** of the Indian Constitution deals with the **application of Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).**
 
• It states that the Directive Principles are **fundamental in the governance of the country** and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
 
• Although DPSPs are not **enforceable by any court**, they are considered essential for achieving the socio-economic objectives outlined in the Constitution.
 
• The Directive Principles aim to ensure **social justice, economic welfare, and political equality** for all citizens.
 
• Some of the key areas covered under DPSPs include **education, healthcare, environment protection, equitable distribution of resources, and promotion of cottage industries.**
 
• These principles are inspired by the **Irish Constitution** and are included in Part IV of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The DPSPs serve as **guiding principles** for the government to create policies and laws that work toward achieving a welfare state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 36**__

 __
 
• **Article 36** defines the term **"State"** as used in Part IV of the Constitution. It includes the **Government and Parliament of India, the Government and Legislature of the States, and all local or other authorities within Indian territory.**
 
 
 
• **Article 38**__
 __
 
• **Article 38** directs the State to strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting a **social order based on justice—social, economic, and political.**
 
• It also emphasizes the reduction of **income inequalities and inequalities in status, facilities, and opportunities.**
 
 
 
• **Article 39**__
 
 
• **Article 39** outlines several specific principles, such as ensuring **adequate means of livelihood for all citizens**, equal pay for equal work, protection of children, and equitable distribution of resources.
 
• This article is pivotal in addressing social and economic disparities within the country.

questions.question: What special status did the Sixty-ninth Amendment Act, 1991 give to Delhi?

options.text: Designated Delhi as the National Capital Territory with a legislative assembly
Brought Delhi under the control of the President through the Governor
Made Delhi a Union Territory without a legislature

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Designated Delhi as the National Capital Territory with a legislative assembly**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Sixty-ninth Amendment Act, 1991** granted Delhi the status of a **National Capital Territory (NCT).**
 
• This amendment enabled Delhi to have its own **legislative assembly** and **Council of Ministers** to manage affairs related to certain subjects.
 
• It introduced **Article 239AA** into the Constitution of India, detailing the structure and functioning of the governance in Delhi.
 
• While Delhi was given a legislative assembly, it remained a **Union Territory**, with its legislative powers limited to specific domains like public order, police, and land under the control of the Union Government.
 
• Delhi's governance is unique as it has a blend of both the **Union Government** and a locally elected assembly, making it distinct from full-fledged states.
 
• The amendment aimed to strike a balance between Delhi's status as the **capital city** and granting it some degree of self-governance.
 
• The Chief Minister of Delhi is the head of the elected government, but the **Lieutenant Governor** retains significant powers and represents the Union Government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Brought Delhi under the control of the President through the Governor**__

 __
 
• Delhi is governed by the **Lieutenant Governor**, who acts as the representative of the President of India, but it is not directly under the control of a Governor as seen in states.
 
• The **Lieutenant Governor** holds administrative authority and works alongside the elected government.
 
 
 
• **Granted full Statehood to Delhi**__
 __
 
• Delhi has not been granted full statehood. It remains a **Union Territory** with partial state-like governance powers.
 
• Matters like **public order, police, and land** are still under the control of the Union Government.
 
 
 
• **Made Delhi a Union Territory without a legislature**__
 
 
• This option is incorrect because the **Sixty-ninth Amendment Act** explicitly provided Delhi with a **legislative assembly** to handle certain subjects.
 
• Delhi's governance model is distinct from a typical Union Territory without legislative powers, such as Chandigarh.

questions.question: What provision was extended under the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Reservation for SC/ST in legislatures**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020** extended the provision for **reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST)** in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.
 
• This reservation was originally provided under **Article 334** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Such reservations were introduced for a period of **70 years** starting from the adoption of the Constitution in 1950.
 
• The amendment extended the reservation for SCs and STs by **10 years**, thereby ensuring these provisions until **2030**.
 
• The primary aim of this provision is to ensure **adequate political representation** for marginalized communities in legislative bodies.
 
• The reservation does not apply to seats in the **Rajya Sabha** and **Legislative Councils**, as these are indirectly elected bodies.
 
• It highlights India’s commitment to **social justice** and the inclusion of disadvantaged communities in the political process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Voting age for elections**__

 __
 
• The **voting age** in India was reduced from **21 years to 18 years** by the **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988**.
 
• This amendment aimed to provide **greater political participation** for the youth of India.
 
• The reduction of voting age applies to elections for the **Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies**.
 
 
 
• **GST Council term**__
 __
 
• The **GST Council** was established under **Article 279A** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It was introduced through the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**.
 
• The Council is responsible for making decisions related to **Goods and Services Tax (GST)**.
 
• There is no specific term for the GST Council as it is a permanent body.
 
 
 
• **Term of the Lok Sabha**__
 
 
• The **term of the Lok Sabha** is defined as **five years** under **Article 83** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Lok Sabha can be dissolved earlier by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
 
• The term can also be extended during a **national emergency** under provisions of Article 352.

questions.question: What provision was introduced by the Sixty-fifth Amendment Act of 1990 for the welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A multi-member National Commission**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Sixty-fifth Amendment Act of 1990 established a **multi-member National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes** to ensure their welfare and development.
 
• This amendment replaced the single Special Officer for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes with a full-fledged **National Commission**.
 
• The commission was tasked with investigating and monitoring matters related to **safeguards provided to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes** under the Constitution.
 
• It also evaluates the progress of various schemes implemented for the **upliftment of SC/ST communities**.
 
• The commission submits annual reports to the President of India, who forwards them to **Parliament** for discussion and action.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes:**

 
 
• These are historically disadvantaged communities recognized in the Indian Constitution for special measures to ensure their social, educational, and economic development.
 
• Scheduled Castes are communities traditionally subjected to social discrimination, while Scheduled Tribes represent indigenous groups living in remote areas.
 
 
 
• **National Commission for Scheduled Castes:**
 
 
• In 2004, the National Commission for SC/ST was bifurcated into **two separate commissions**: the National Commission for Scheduled Castes and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes.
 
• The National Commission for Scheduled Castes focuses exclusively on issues related to Scheduled Castes.
 
 
 
• **National Commission for Scheduled Tribes:**
 
 
• The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes was established under Article 338A of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It monitors safeguards related to STs, advises on policies, and evaluates the development of tribal communities.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Safeguards for SC/ST:**
 
 
• Article 46: Promotes educational and economic interests of SCs/STs.
 
• Article 17: Abolishes "untouchability" and forbids its practice.
 
• Article 15(4): Allows the state to make special provisions for SCs/STs in education.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India prohibits human trafficking?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 23**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 23** of the Indian Constitution explicitly prohibits human trafficking, forced labor, and other forms of exploitation.
 
• This provision applies to both citizens and non-citizens, ensuring universal protection against exploitation.
 
• Under Article 23, acts such as begar (compulsory labor without payment) are outlawed, emphasizing dignity and equality.
 
• Article 23 is enforceable by law, and violations can lead to punitive actions under relevant legislations such as the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.
 
• This article is a part of the Fundamental Rights section, which guarantees civil liberties to all individuals against state and private exploitation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Human Trafficking:**

 
 
• Refers to the illegal trade of humans for exploitation such as forced labor, sexual slavery, or commercial sexual exploitation.
 
• Globally recognized as a serious crime and violation of human rights under international laws such as the Palermo Protocol.
 
 
 
• **Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956:**
 
 
• A key legislation in India aimed at preventing and combating human trafficking.
 
• Provides measures for rescue, rehabilitation, and prosecution of offenders involved in trafficking.
 
 
 
• **Article 24:**
 
 
• Prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in hazardous occupations such as factories and mines.
 
• Complements Article 23 by addressing exploitation specific to child labor.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• Article 23 is a part of the Fundamental Rights enshrined in Part III of the Constitution.
 
• These rights are enforceable by the judiciary and protect against exploitation and discrimination.

questions.question: Judicial review is essential to:

options.text: uphold the supremacy of the Constitution

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**uphold the supremacy of the Constitution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Judicial review is a mechanism to ensure that laws and executive actions comply with the provisions of the Constitution, thereby upholding its supremacy.
 
• It empowers the judiciary to invalidate laws or actions by the legislature and executive if they violate constitutional principles.
 
• The concept of judicial review is derived from the principle of the separation of powers and checks and balances in governance.
 
• Judicial review safeguards fundamental rights and ensures accountability of the government to constitutional norms.
 
• This principle is integral to democratic governance and prevents arbitrary use of power by any branch of the government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Review:**

 
 
• The term refers to the authority of the courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative acts and executive decisions.
 
• Judicial review originated in the United States through the landmark case **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
 
• In India, judicial review is an essential feature of the Constitution under Articles **13, 32, and 226**.
 
• It is a part of the basic structure doctrine established by the Supreme Court in the **Keshavananda Bharati case (1973)**.
 
 
 
• **Supremacy of the Constitution:**
 
 
• The Constitution is the highest legal authority in India, and all laws and actions must conform to it.
 
• Article 141 ensures that judgments of the Supreme Court are binding on all courts in India.
 
• The concept reinforces the rule of law and prevents autocratic governance.
 
 
 
• **Separation of Powers:**
 
 
• It is a governance principle dividing powers among the legislature, executive, and judiciary.
 
• Judicial review acts as a check on the legislature and executive to maintain balance.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• Judicial review ensures protection against violations of fundamental rights enshrined under Part III of the Constitution.
 
• Examples include the right to equality, freedom of speech, and protection against discrimination.

questions.question: The concept of Lok Adalat draws inspiration from the _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**ancient Indian dispute resolution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lok Adalat is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism inspired by the **ancient Indian system of dispute resolution**, which emphasized amicable settlement of conflicts through dialogue and consensus.
 
• The concept is rooted in traditional practices such as **panchayats** and public assemblies where disputes were resolved by community leaders or elders.
 
• The modern Lok Adalat system was institutionalized in India under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** to provide an informal and cost-effective mechanism for dispute resolution.
 
• Lok Adalats are organized by **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** and State Legal Services Authorities to ensure justice is accessible to all, especially marginalized communities.
 
• These courts have the power to resolve cases related to civil disputes, matrimonial issues, and compoundable criminal cases, with decisions being legally binding on the parties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**

 
 
• This Act provides the framework for the establishment of Lok Adalats across India.
 
• Under the Act, awards made by Lok Adalats are final, binding, and enforceable as decrees of a civil court.
 
• The Act aims to ensure free legal aid and promote justice for weaker sections of society.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Lok Adalat**
 
 
• Cases resolved in Lok Adalats are settled amicably without any lengthy litigation process.
 
• Parties are not required to pay court fees, and if a case is settled in Lok Adalat, the court fee paid earlier is refunded.
 
• These courts are known for their simplicity and speedy resolution of disputes.
 
 
 
• **Panchayat System in Ancient India**
 
 
• In ancient India, village-level panchayats were responsible for resolving disputes through collective wisdom and consensus.
 
• Panchayats emphasized fairness, impartiality, and community welfare in their decisions.
 
 
 
• **Role of National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)**
 
 
• NALSA was constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act to oversee and implement legal services programs across India.
 
• It plays a key role in organizing Lok Adalats and ensuring justice delivery to underprivileged groups.

questions.question: What happens if a municipality in India is dissolved before completing its full term?

options.text: The previous municipal council is reinstated.
The central government takes over governance.
A new election must be held within 6 months

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A new election must be held within 6 months**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• If a municipality in India is dissolved before completing its five-year term, **a new election must be held within six months**, as per Article 243U of the Indian Constitution.
 
• This provision ensures the continuity of local self-governance and prevents prolonged governance gaps.
 
• However, if the remaining term of the dissolved municipality is less than six months, elections are not mandatory.
 
• The State Election Commission is responsible for conducting these elections in accordance with the constitutional mandate.
 
• During the interim period, the state government may appoint an administrator or a special officer to manage the municipality's affairs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 243U:**

 
 
• It specifies the duration of municipalities, setting a fixed term of five years from the date of their first meeting.
 
• It mandates that elections must be conducted before the expiration of the term or within six months of dissolution.
 
 
 
• **State Election Commission (SEC):**
 
 
• A constitutional body empowered to supervise, direct, and control municipal and panchayat elections at the state level.
 
• It operates independently of the Election Commission of India.
 
 
 
• **Municipality:**
 
 
• It is an urban local body established to govern a city or town with a population exceeding a specified threshold.
 
• It functions under the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
 
 
 
• **Interim Administration:**
 
 
• Upon municipal dissolution, the state government may appoint an administrator to oversee day-to-day operations until elections are held.
 
• This ensures that essential public services and governance functions continue uninterrupted.

questions.question: Which principle of citizenship did India start following more strictly after the 2003 Amendment?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Jus sanguinis (by blood)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• After the **2003 Amendment** to the **Citizenship Act, 1955**, India shifted from the principle of **jus soli (citizenship by birth)** to a stricter application of **jus sanguinis (citizenship by descent).**
 
• The amendment introduced stricter conditions for acquiring Indian citizenship, especially for children born in India to foreign nationals.
 
• The focus was shifted to emphasize **ancestral ties**, meaning citizenship was granted based on the nationality of the parents rather than the place of birth.
 
• Under the revised law, a person born in India after **December 3, 2004**, can only claim Indian citizenship if at least one parent is an Indian citizen and the other parent is not an illegal migrant.
 
• The amendment aimed to address concerns over **illegal immigration** and its impact on demography and national security, especially in border states.
 
• The principle of **jus sanguinis** aligns with the concept of maintaining a closer connection to the nation through family lineage.
 
• This change brought India's citizenship laws more in line with countries that prioritize **descent-based citizenship**, such as Germany and Japan.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Jus soli (by birth)**__

 __
 
• The principle of **jus soli** grants citizenship to anyone born within a country's territory, regardless of their parents' nationality.
 
• Prior to the 2003 Amendment, India followed this principle for granting citizenship. For example, anyone born in India between **1950** and **1987** was automatically considered an Indian citizen.
 
• However, concerns over **illegal immigration** led to restrictions on this principle starting from **1987**, and it was further curtailed in the **2003 Amendment**.
 
• Countries like the **United States** still follow the principle of jus soli, granting automatic citizenship to anyone born on their soil.
 
 
 
• **Dual citizenship**__
 __
 
• India does not allow **dual citizenship**. The **Citizenship Act, 1955** mandates that Indian citizens must renounce their citizenship if they acquire the citizenship of another country.
 
• However, India allows individuals of Indian origin living abroad to obtain an **Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card**, which provides certain privileges without granting full citizenship.
 
• Dual citizenship is practiced in some countries like **Canada** and the **United Kingdom**, allowing individuals to hold citizenship in more than one country simultaneously.
 
 
 
• **Universal citizenship**__
 
 
• The concept of **universal citizenship** refers to the idea that all individuals belong to a global community and should have equal rights and opportunities regardless of their country of origin.
 
• This concept is more philosophical and is not implemented by any country in its legal framework.
 
• It contrasts with the traditional notions of citizenship, which are tied to national borders and sovereignty.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India states about the directive for states to make provision for public assistance in cases of unemployment?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 41**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 41** of the Constitution of India is a part of the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which are enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution.
 
• It directs the state to make effective provisions for **securing the right to work, education, and public assistance** in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and other cases of undeserved want.
 
• The provision under Article 41 is **non-justiciable**, meaning it cannot be enforced by courts, but it acts as a guiding principle for the state while formulating policies.
 
• Article 41 emphasizes the responsibility of the state to consider its **economic capacity and development** while implementing these provisions.
 
• The **Directive Principles of State Policy** aim to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order informed by justice—social, economic, and political.
 
• Article 41 is particularly relevant in addressing **social and economic inequalities**, ensuring that vulnerable sections of society receive adequate support.
 
• The article complements other provisions like **Article 39**, which focus on equitable distribution of resources, and **Article 42**, which deals with just and humane conditions of work.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• ** Article 39**__

 __
 
• **Article 39** is also a part of the Directive Principles of State Policy.
 
• It mandates the state to ensure that the **ownership and control of material resources** of the community are distributed to serve the common good.
 
• It also emphasizes preventing the concentration of wealth and means of production to the detriment of the common interest.
 
• Additionally, Article 39 focuses on providing children with opportunities to develop in a healthy manner and protecting them against exploitation.
 
 
 
• **Article 42**__
 __
 
• **Article 42** directs the state to make provisions for securing **just and humane conditions of work** and for maternity relief.
 
• This article aims to improve the quality of labor conditions and is particularly significant for the welfare of women and workers.
 
• It complements labor laws and policies, ensuring social justice for working individuals.
 
 
 
• **Article 40**__
 
 
• **Article 40** deals with the organization of **village panchayats**.
 
• It directs the state to take steps to organize village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as **units of self-government**.
 
• This article is crucial for strengthening **grassroots democracy** in India.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key reason for judicial review in India?

options.text: To allow the judiciary to make laws
To maintain federal balance between Centre and States
To ensure the supremacy of the Parliament
To protect the supremacy of the Constitution and fundamental rights

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**To protect the supremacy of the Constitution and fundamental rights**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Judicial review** in India ensures the protection of the **supremacy of the Constitution**, which is the highest law of the land.
 
• It is a mechanism for safeguarding **fundamental rights**, as guaranteed under **Part III of the Indian Constitution**, against legislative and executive actions.
 
• The judiciary has the authority to review the actions and decisions of the legislature and executive to ensure they do not violate the **Constitutional provisions**.
 
• Judicial review enables the courts to declare laws or actions null and void if they are inconsistent with the Constitution.
 
• It upholds the principle of **constitutional morality**, ensuring that all laws and policies align with the values and principles enshrined in the Constitution.
 
• This process helps maintain the balance between the various organs of the government, preventing any one organ from exceeding its powers.
 
• Judicial review is crucial in a democracy like India, where the judiciary acts as the **guardian of the Constitution** and the rights of citizens.
 
• The concept finds its roots in **Articles 13, 32, and 226** of the Indian Constitution, which empower the judiciary to review laws and protect fundamental rights.
 
• It is especially significant in cases involving the violation of rights such as **freedom of speech**, **equality**, and **personal liberty**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• ** To allow the judiciary to make laws**__

 __
 
• The judiciary does not have the power to **legislate**; its role is limited to interpreting and applying the law as per the Constitution.
 
• Law-making is the exclusive domain of the **legislature** in India, as per the separation of powers principle.
 
• Judicial review does not involve creating laws but reviewing them for **Constitutional validity**.
 
 
 
• **To maintain federal balance between Centre and States**__
 __
 
• While judicial review does play a role in resolving disputes between the **Centre and States**, this is not its primary purpose.
 
• Federal balance is maintained through mechanisms like the **Finance Commission** and specific provisions in the Constitution, such as **Article 246**, detailing the division of legislative powers.
 
 
 
• **To ensure the supremacy of the Parliament**__
 
 
• In India, the **Constitution**, not the Parliament, is supreme, unlike in the UK where parliamentary sovereignty exists.
 
• The judiciary reviews parliamentary laws to ensure they align with the **Constitutional framework**.
 
• Judicial review acts as a check on parliamentary supremacy, ensuring that laws do not violate **fundamental rights**.

questions.question: Which body primarily exercises the powers delegated through Article 243W of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Municipal Corporations**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Article 243W of the Indian Constitution provides for the **functional responsibilities and powers** of **Municipalities**, which include **Municipal Corporations**, **Municipal Councils**, and **Nagar Panchayats**.
 
• The article is part of the **74th Constitutional Amendment Act**, which introduced the concept of urban local governance in India.
 
• The functions under Article 243W include the preparation of plans for economic development and social justice, implementation of schemes, and responsibilities related to **urban infrastructure and services**, such as water supply, sanitation, and urban planning.
 
• **Municipal Corporations** are established in larger cities and are responsible for urban development, governance, and providing essential services such as **roads, education, health care, waste management, and street lighting.**
 
• The powers and responsibilities delegated to Municipal Corporations are outlined in the **12th Schedule** of the Constitution, which includes **18 functional areas**, such as urban planning, regulation of land use, slum improvement, public health, and more.
 
• The **State Legislature** is responsible for defining the powers, authority, and responsibilities of Municipalities under Article 243W.
 
• Municipal Corporations ensure the implementation of policies and schemes at the urban level, contributing to **decentralized governance** as envisaged by the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Parliament of India**__

 __
 
• The **Parliament of India** is the supreme legislative body in the country and consists of the **Lok Sabha** and the **Rajya Sabha**.
 
• Its role is to enact laws and policies, including constitutional amendments such as the **73rd and 74th Amendments**, which introduced Panchayati Raj and urban local bodies.
 
• While the Parliament provides a framework for governance, it does not directly exercise powers under Article 243W; these are delegated to urban local bodies like Municipal Corporations.
 
 
 
• **Panchayati Raj Institutions**__
 __
 
• **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)** are responsible for rural governance and exercise powers under **Article 243G**, not Article 243W.
 
• PRIs operate at three levels: **Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti,** and **Zila Parishad**, focusing on rural development and decentralized governance.
 
• They handle functions related to **agriculture, rural infrastructure, and poverty alleviation**, as outlined in the **11th Schedule** of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **State Legislature**__
 
 
• The **State Legislature** plays a critical role in defining the powers, authority, and responsibilities of Municipal Corporations and other urban local bodies under Article 243W.
 
• It establishes laws and frameworks for governance at the urban level, including the enactment of state-specific **Municipal Acts**.
 
• However, it does not directly exercise the powers delegated under Article 243W; it delegates these to the urban local bodies.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India prohibits Indian citizens from accepting any title from a foreign state?
questions.solution:
Source Code:

The correct answer is __**Article 18**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 18 of the Constitution of India prohibits Indian citizens from accepting titles from foreign states.
 
• It forms part of the fundamental rights under the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18).
 
• This provision ensures the abolition of titles that create artificial distinctions within society.
 
• The Article states that no citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign state while holding any office of profit or trust under the government.
 
• However, military and academic distinctions are exempted from this prohibition.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution of India.
 
• They are classified into six categories: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right Against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
• Articles 14-18 collectively form the Right to Equality.
 
 
 
• **Abolition of Titles:**
 
 
• Article 18(1) abolishes all titles except military or academic distinctions.
 
• It was aimed at eliminating practices like conferring "Sir" or other hereditary titles that signify class distinction.
 
 
 
• **International Context:**
 
 
• Many countries have provisions restricting or regulating the acceptance of foreign titles by their citizens.
 
• Such measures are often aimed at maintaining sovereignty and avoiding conflicts of interest.
 
 
 
• **Historical Background:**
 
 
• The abolition of titles was influenced by the freedom movement, where leaders opposed titles granted by British colonial rulers.
 
• Titles like "Rai Bahadur" and "Khan Bahadur" were seen as symbols of loyalty to the British regime.

questions.question: What is a major drawback of the parliamentary system in terms of governance stability?

options.text: Elections are held only once every decade.
The President can dismiss the Prime Minister at any time.
The judiciary frequently overrules executive decisions
Governments may collapse due to no-confidence motions or coalition disputes

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Governments may collapse due to no-confidence motions or coalition disputes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In parliamentary systems, governments are often formed by coalitions, which can be unstable due to conflicting interests among coalition partners.
 
• A no-confidence motion is a parliamentary procedure that allows members to vote on whether they continue to support the government, and its passage can lead to government collapse.
 
• Frequent disputes between coalition parties or failure to maintain majority support can result in political instability and snap elections.
 
• Such instability can disrupt long-term policy-making and governance, affecting the nation's economic and social progress.
 
• Countries with parliamentary systems, such as India and Italy, have experienced instances where coalition disputes have led to frequent changes in government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Coalition Government:**

 
 
• A government formed by multiple political parties, often seen in parliamentary systems where no single party has a majority.
 
• While it promotes representation of diverse viewpoints, it can also lead to disagreements and policy deadlock.
 
 
 
• **No-Confidence Motion:**
 
 
• A formal vote in the legislature to determine if the current government has the support of the majority of members.
 
• If passed, it typically results in the resignation of the Prime Minister and the dissolution of the government.
 
 
 
• **Snap Elections:**
 
 
• Elections called earlier than expected due to political instability, often following a government collapse.
 
• They can be costly and disrupt governance, but are necessary to restore stability and legitimacy.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary System:**
 
 
• A form of government where the executive is derived from the legislative branch and is accountable to it.
 
• The Prime Minister is typically the leader of the majority party or coalition in parliament.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Instability:**
 
 
• Italy has experienced over 60 governments since World War II due to coalition disputes.
 
• India has also faced instances of government collapse during coalition eras, particularly in the 1990s.

questions.question: In India, what are municipalities primarily responsible for?

options.text: Administration of small cities or towns

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Administration of small cities or towns**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Municipalities** in India are urban local bodies responsible for the administration and development of small cities or towns under their jurisdiction.
 
• They are established under the **74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**, which provides a framework for decentralized governance in urban areas.
 
• Key functions include urban planning, public health, sanitation, water supply, waste management, and infrastructure development for small cities or towns.
 
• Municipalities generate revenue through property tax, municipal bonds, grants from the state government, and user fees for services.
 
• They are governed by elected representatives and operate through standing committees and administrative staff to ensure efficient service delivery.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Urban Local Bodies in India:**

 
 
• Municipal Corporations: Govern large urban areas with a population exceeding 1 million.
 
• Municipal Councils: Administer smaller cities or towns with a population between 25,000 and 1 million.
 
• Nagar Panchayats: Manage transitional areas moving from rural to urban.
 
 
 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act:**
 
 
• Introduced in 1992, it aims to strengthen local self-governance in urban areas.
 
• Mandates the formation of municipalities, wards committees, and state finance commissions.
 
• Defines 18 functional items under the 12th Schedule for urban local bodies, including urban planning and poverty alleviation.
 
 
 
• **Revenue Sources for Municipalities:**
 
 
• Property tax, water tax, and user charges for municipal services.
 
• Grants from the central and state governments.
 
• Revenue from municipal bonds and public-private partnerships (PPPs).
 
 
 
• **Challenges Faced by Municipalities:**
 
 
• Limited financial autonomy and dependency on state governments for funds.
 
• Inadequate infrastructure and service delivery due to rapid urbanization.
 
• Lack of skilled manpower and efficient governance mechanisms.
 
 
 
• **Smart Cities Mission:**
 
 
• Launched in 2015 by the Government of India to promote sustainable and inclusive urban development.
 
• Aims to transform selected cities into smart cities by improving infrastructure, governance, and technology integration.

questions.question: How can a foreigner who has lived in India for 12 years acquire Indian citizenship?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By naturalisation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Indian citizenship can be acquired by a foreigner who has resided in India for a continuous period of **12 years** under the provisions of the **Citizenship Act, 1955**.
 
• The process is known as **naturalisation**, which is detailed in Section 6 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
 
• To be eligible, the individual must have resided in India for **11 years cumulatively** in the 14 years preceding the application and for **12 months continuously** before submitting the application.
 
• The applicant must also meet specific qualifications, such as **good character**, adequate knowledge of an Indian language, and renunciation of citizenship of the foreign country.
 
• Upon successful application, citizenship is granted by a certificate issued by the **Government of India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Citizenship Act, 1955:**

 
 
• The Citizenship Act, 1955, governs the acquisition, termination, and supplementary provisions of Indian citizenship.
 
• It provides five methods for acquiring citizenship: by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory.
 
 
 
• **Naturalisation vs Registration:**
 
 
• Naturalisation is for foreigners who meet the residency and other criteria, while registration is for specific categories like persons of Indian origin (PIOs) or spouses of Indian citizens.
 
• Registration requires a shorter residency period compared to naturalisation.
 
 
 
• **Language Requirement:**
 
 
• The applicant must have adequate knowledge of at least one of the **official languages of India** as specified in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Renunciation of Previous Citizenship:**
 
 
• India does not allow dual citizenship; therefore, an individual must renounce their previous citizenship to acquire Indian citizenship via naturalisation.
 
 
 
• **Good Character Criterion:**
 
 
• The applicant must demonstrate good moral character, verified through background checks during the application process.

questions.question: Why does the parliamentary system prevent executive despotism?

options.text: Because the Prime Minister has unlimited power
Because the judiciary can override executive decisions without checks
Because executive authority is dispersed among a group of ministers accountable to the Parliament
Because the military can intervene in governance

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Because executive authority is dispersed among a group of ministers accountable to the Parliament**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **parliamentary system ensures that the executive authority is not concentrated in one individual** but is collectively shared by a cabinet of ministers.
 
• Ministers in the executive are accountable to the Parliament, which acts as a check against any form of authoritarianism or unilateral decision-making.
 
• The **Prime Minister and cabinet members can be questioned, censured, or removed** through parliamentary mechanisms such as votes of no confidence.
 
• This system promotes transparency and prevents the abuse of executive power by subjecting it to parliamentary oversight and democratic processes.
 
• The dispersal of power among various ministers prevents despotism and ensures collective decision-making aligned with public interests.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Parliamentary Democracy:**

 
 
• A system of government where the executive branch derives its legitimacy from the legislative branch and is accountable to it.
 
• Examples include the UK, India, and Canada.
 
 
 
• **Vote of No Confidence:**
 
 
• A parliamentary procedure used to remove a government or executive by showing that it no longer has the majority support of the legislature.
 
• It is an essential tool to ensure executive accountability in a parliamentary system.
 
 
 
• **Separation of Powers:**
 
 
• A principle where governmental powers are divided among different branches: executive, legislative, and judiciary.
 
• In a parliamentary system, the executive and legislature are closely linked, unlike in a presidential system where they are separate.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Oversight:**
 
 
• The judiciary in parliamentary democracies can review executive actions to ensure compliance with the Constitution.
 
• This further prevents authoritarian tendencies in governance.
 
 
 
• **Collective Responsibility:**
 
 
• A principle in parliamentary systems where all cabinet members share responsibility for decisions and policies of the government.
 
• This ensures accountability and prevents individual despotism within the executive.

questions.question: In which of the following cases did the court restrict the Parliament from curtailing any Fundamental Right?

options.text: Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala
A K Gopalan vs State of Madras

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Golaknath vs State of Punjab**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **In Golaknath vs State of Punjab**, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament cannot curtail or amend Fundamental Rights under the Constitution.
 
• The court held that Fundamental Rights are transcendental and cannot be abridged by ordinary legislation.
 
• This judgment restricted Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368.
 
• **Later,** in the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)**, Parliament was allowed to amend the Constitution but not in a way that destroys its basic structure, including Fundamental Rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine:**

 
 
• Introduced in the Kesavananda Bharati case, it holds that certain fundamental features of the Constitution cannot be altered or destroyed through amendments.
 
• Examples of such features include the supremacy of the Constitution, secularism, democracy, and judicial independence.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• These are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution and guarantee civil liberties such as equality, freedom, and protection against exploitation.
 
• They ensure that Indian citizens can live with dignity and freedom within the framework of the law.
 
 
 
• **24th Constitutional Amendment:**
 
 
• Passed in 1971, it empowered Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
 
• This amendment was challenged in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Review:**
 
 
• This refers to the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions.
 
• It was reaffirmed in the Kesavananda Bharati case as a feature of the Basic Structure.
 
 
 
• **Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967):**
 
 
• In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights.
 
• This decision was later modified by the Kesavananda Bharati judgment, which allowed amendments but restricted them under the Basic Structure Doctrine.
